readmeExcerpt:
# inbrowser-ai

[![CI](https://github.com/Superactive-AI/inbrowser-ai/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Superactive-AI/inbrowser-ai/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@superactive/inbrowser-ai.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@superactive/inbrowser-ai)
[![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](./LICENSE)

**Run speech-to-text, an LLM, and text-to-speech in the browser, any of
them, on their own or wired together into one voice pipeline.** No server,
no GPU to rent, no API key of your own to host: on-device speech
recognition (Whisper), an LLM (transformers.js, or any OpenRouter model),
and on-device text-to-speech (Kokoro), each usable standalone or combined
into a streaming voice pipeline that runs on WebGPU in the visitor's own
browser tab.

Whisper, Kokoro, and the on-device LLM all require **WebGPU**: WASM
inference for models at this scale is too slow for conversational latency,
so this package doesn't offer it as a fallback. The one exception is VAD
(Silero), a tiny per-frame speech/silence classifier, unrelated to that
bottleneck, which stays on WASM by design. Browsers without WebGPU still
work through the Web Speech STT/TTS engines.

[**Try the live demo**](https://superactive-ai.github.io/inbrowser-ai/), no
install, just a browser tab.

```
mic -> VAD (Silero) -> STT (Whisper | Web Speech)
    -> [your reply source] -> TTS (Kokoro | Web Speech) -> speakers
```

That's the full pipeline, but every piece also works alone: use just STT to
transcribe audio, just TTS to speak text, just the LLM to generate a reply,
in whatever combination your product actually needs. The models run on the
visitor's own device, so the only real cost is the one-time download of the
weights themselves, cached afterward so every later session loads
near-instantly.

## Why this exists

Running STT, an LLM, and TTS usually means separate API calls to separate
hosted services, each with its own latency, its own bill, and its own
privacy trade-off (the audio and the conversation both leave the device).
inbrowser-ai takes the opposite bet: ship the models to the browser instead,
and get

- **No server cost that scales with usage**, since every user's device does
  the work, so a viral spike in traffic doesn't turn into a viral spike in
  your inference bill.
- **Low latency once cached**, since there's no network round-trip to a
  model host for STT/TTS, and replies stream sentence by sentence so speech
  starts before the full response has even finished generating.
- **Privacy by construction**, since audio and conversation text never
  have to leave the device unless you explicitly choose a server-hosted
  reply source.
- **Nothing to provision**, since there are no GPU instances to size or
  keep warm; the models simply aren't running when nobody's using them.

The trade-off is real too: first-run downloads (tens to hundreds of MB
depending on the models picked), and the end user's device does the
compute, so results scale with their hardware, not yours. inbrowser-ai is
built for the products where that trade-off is the right one: voice
companions, on-device assistants, accessibility tooling, demos, anything
where "runs anywhere, costs nothing to scale" matters more than
"guaranteed server-grade throughput."

inbrowser-ai itself has no knowledge of any particular app, character, or
backend. It only knows about: browser capability detection, engine
implementations, model downloading/caching, and debug instrumentation. An
app wires the pieces into its own session logic, or just drops in the
included `VoicePlayground` component to get a full working demo/debug UI
for free.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superactive/inbrowser-ai
```

This ships as TypeScript source, not a compiled `dist/`. Every engine's Web
Worker is created with `new URL("./x.worker.ts", import.meta.url)`, a
pattern that only resolves correctly when a bundler processes the package's
own sou

name: sreerevanth/groq-voice-assistant
readmeExcerpt:
# ⚡ Groq Voice Assistant — Sub-500ms Voice Pipeline

A production-grade, real-time voice AI assistant leveraging **Groq's LPU (Language Processing Unit)** for deterministic, ultra-low-latency inference. The system targets a complete voice round-trip under **500ms**.

---

## Architecture

```
Browser (TypeScript/Vite)
│
│  MediaRecorder + Web Audio API (VAD)
│        │  WebSocket (binary PCM audio)
│        ▼
FastAPI Backend (Python asyncio)
│
├── Stage 1: STT  ── Groq Whisper API    ~100–200ms
├── Stage 2: LLM  ── Groq LPU (Llama)    ~50–150ms  ← streaming TTFT
└── Stage 3: TTS  ── OpenAI / ElevenLabs ~80–200ms
        │
        │  WebSocket (base64 MP3)
        ▼
Browser AudioContext → Speaker
```

### Latency Budget

| Stage | Model/Service | Target |
|---|---|---|
| STT (Whisper) | `whisper-large-v3-turbo` on Groq | 100–200 ms |
| LLM TTFT | `llama-3.1-8b-instant` on Groq LPU | 50–100 ms |
| LLM Full | Token streaming, ~128 tok | 80–150 ms |
| TTS | ElevenLabs turbo / OpenAI tts-1 | 80–200 ms |
| **Total** | | **< 500 ms** |

**Key metric definitions:**
- **TTFT** (Time-to-First-Token): latency from prompt submission to first LLM token received. Critical for perceived responsiveness.
- **TPOT** (Time-per-Output-Token): measures LLM throughput; Groq LPU achieves ~500–800 tok/s vs ~60 tok/s on standard GPUs.

---

## Skills Demonstrated

### 1. Real-time Systems
- Full latency budget tracking (TTFT, TPOT, STT, TTS, end-to-end)
- Sentence-boundary detection for early TTS dispatch (pipeline parallelism)
- WebSocket binary frame streaming for audio transport

### 2. Audio Processing
- Browser `MediaRecorder` capturing PCM at 16kHz, mono, with echo cancellation
- Voice Activity Detection (VAD) via Web Audio `AnalyserNode` RMS energy
- Automatic silence detection + utterance segmentation (walkie-talkie mode)
- Server-side WAV encoding for Whisper API ingestion
- Multi-provider TTS: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Microsoft Edge TTS (fallback)
- `AudioContext.decodeAudioData()` + queued `AudioBufferSourceNode` playback

### 3. Concurrency (Python asyncio)
- `AsyncGroq` client — all I/O non-blocking
- Async generator pattern for LLM token streaming
- Sentence buffer: TTS starts on first complete sentence while LLM continues
- Multiple sessions handled concurrently via asyncio event loop
- `uvloop` event loop backend (2–4× faster than CPython default)

### 4. WebSocket / Realtime APIs
- Multiplexed WebSocket: JSON control events + binary audio frames on same connection
- Server-sent event types: `transcript`, `llm_token`, `llm_sentence`, `audio`, `metrics`
- Graceful reconnection and session state management
- Ping/pong latency measurement built in

### 5. API Integration
- **Groq SDK** (`AsyncGroq`): Whisper transcription + LLaMA chat completion
- **OpenAI REST** (`httpx` async): TTS-1 synthesis
- **ElevenLabs streaming** API: eleven_turbo_v2 model
- **Microsoft Edge TTS** (`edge-tts`): zero-cost fallback

---

## Project Structure

```
groq-voice-assistant/
├── backend/
│   ├── main.py              # FastAPI app, WebSocket endpoint, pipeline orchestration
│   ├── requirements.txt     # Python deps
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   └── .env.example         # API keys config
│
├── frontend/
│   ├── index.html           # App shell
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── pipeline.ts      # VoicePipelineClient + AudioPlayer classes
│   │   └── main.ts          # UI logic, state machine, DOM bindings
│   ├── vite.config.ts
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── package.json
│
└── docker-compose.yml
```

---

## Setup

### Prerequisites
- Python 3.12+
- Node.js 20+
- [Groq API key](https://console.groq.com) (free tier works)
- Chrome or Edge browser (MediaRecorder + WebAudio)

### 1. Backend

```bash
cd backend

# Create virtualenv
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate       # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install deps
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Configure keys
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env → set GROQ_API_KEY (required)
#              set OPENAI_API_KEY + TTS

# NutriCoach Voice Agent

Multichannel voice agent for **nutritional coaching**: meal tracking, health goals, advice on supplements and physical activity — using function calling, Karpathy-style document RAG with graph expansion + BM25 + Italian stemming, free-tier multi-provider LLM routing, **realtime voice via WebSocket** with STT streaming, sentence-progressive TTS, and barge-in.

Portfolio project showcasing: from-scratch agentic system (zero framework), bidirectional streaming (WebSocket + SSE), streaming STT (Deepgram Nova-3), progressive TTS per sentence, deterministic ranked-BM25 RAG, safety layers (input guardrails, PII masking, tool validator, escalation gate, retry), per-request provider selection.

Voice-to-voice latency target: **800ms–1.2s** (cascaded streaming pattern, LiveKit/Pipecat 2026 best practice).

---

## Architecture

```

WhatsApp / Telegram ─► POST /webhooks/{wa,tg} ─► normalize → pipeline (HMAC verified)

                  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

name: gateniomer/whisper-browser
readmeExcerpt:
# Scribe

On-device speech-to-text that runs entirely in the browser. Scribe listens to
your microphone, transcribes live, and never sends your audio anywhere — the
models run locally with WebGPU (or CPU/WASM) and work offline once downloaded.

> The repository is named `whisper-browser` for historical reasons; the app is
> called **Scribe** because it isn't tied to a single model.

## Features

- **Live transcription** with timestamped, append-only lines.
- **Fully local** — audio never leaves the device; no accounts, no servers, no
  telemetry.
- **Multiple models** (Whisper, Moonshine, Distil-Whisper) with an in-app
  download manager — pick what to download and delete it anytime. Downloaded
  models show **Use** to load and **Unload** (eject) to free memory without
  deleting the files.
- **WebGPU accelerated**, with an automatic CPU (WASM) fallback, and a clear
  indicator when the GPU isn't available.
- **Works offline** after a model is cached in the browser.
- **Mobile-first UI**: one big mic button, live input meter, timer, and a
  settings sheet.
- **No backend.** Deploy it as a static site.

## Supported models

Sizes are approximate download sizes for the two ONNX files, which differ by
backend (WebGPU uses higher precision; CPU uses 8-bit).

| Model | Params | Size | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Whisper Tiny | 39M | ~41 MB | multilingual, fastest Whisper (GPU/CPU) |
| Whisper Base | 74M | ~77 MB | multilingual, balanced (GPU/CPU) |
| Whisper Small | 244M | ~249 MB | multilingual, more accurate (GPU/CPU) |
| Whisper Large v3 Turbo | 809M | ~1.1 GB | multilingual; runs on CPU |
| Moonshine Tiny | 27M | ~28 MB | English, built for real-time (GPU/CPU) |
| Moonshine Base | 61M | ~63 MB | English, real-time (GPU/CPU) |
| Distil-Whisper Large v3.5 | 756M | ~1.0 GB | English; ~6x faster than large-v3; runs on CPU |
| Cohere Transcribe | 2B | ~2.1 GB | 14 languages, best-in-class accuracy; **requires WebGPU** |
| Parakeet TDT 0.6B v2 | 600M | ~0.7 GB | English, top accuracy (experimental) |
| Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 | 600M | ~0.7 GB | 25 European languages (experimental) |

Whisper and Distil-Whisper are multilingual/English batch models driven in a
low-latency streaming fashion (voice-activity segmentation). Moonshine is
designed for live transcription and feels the most responsive.

GPU sizes are `fp32` (Cohere uses `q4`); CPU sizes are 8-bit (`q8`). Large
Whisper-family models run on the CPU: their fp32 encoder is external data
(~2.5 GB, too big for the browser) and their 4-bit WebGPU kernels are unreliable
for Whisper, so Scribe uses the accurate q8 CPU weights instead. Cohere
Transcribe runs only on **WebGPU** (its quantized embeddings use the
`GatherBlockQuantized` op, which the CPU/WASM provider doesn't implement).

**Engine architecture.** Models are hosted behind pluggable engines
(`src/lib/engines/`): Transformers.js (Whisper/Moonshine/Cohere) and parakeet.js
(Parakeet). The router in `src/lib/engine.js` picks one per model family, so
adding a runtime doesn't touch the app. Parakeet is experimental; it caches in
IndexedDB, which Scribe reads directly (`engines/parakeetCache.js`) so per-model
Downloaded/Delete work without touching other models.

## How it works

1. **Capture** — an `AudioWorklet` (`src/worklet/pcm-worklet.js`) streams 16 kHz
   mono PCM from the microphone.
2. **Segment** — an energy-based VAD with an adaptive noise floor, hysteresis,
   pre-roll and trailing-silence trimming groups speech into short utterances.
3. **Transcribe** — each utterance goes to Transformers.js, which runs the model
   through ONNX Runtime Web.
4. **Engine placement** — the engine runs in a Web Worker when the worker
   exposes WebGPU (e.g. Chrome); otherwise it runs on the main thread if only the
   window exposes WebGPU (e.g. Firefox/Safari); otherwise it stays in the worker
   on CPU. This is decided once at startup.
5. **Cache** — models are stored in a dedicated `CacheStorage` cache
   (`whisper-models`) that

name: samsgates/local-voice-agent
readmeExcerpt:
# Local-Voice-Agent

A browser-first, local AI voice-agent framework combining browser VAD, local/WebGPU speech-to-text, WebGPU language models, local/WebGPU text-to-speech, barge-in, tools, memory, local RAG, device benchmarking, and latency telemetry behind one TypeScript API.

![Features](media_resources/features.png)

## Architecture

![Architecture Diagram](media_resources/architech_diagram.png)

```text
Microphone
   │
   ▼
@ricky0123/vad-web (Silero v5)
   │ 16 kHz Float32 speech segment
   ▼
STT router
   ├─ Browser on-device SpeechRecognition
   ├─ Whisper Tiny/Base via Transformers.js
   └─ Moonshine via Transformers.js
   │
   ▼
LocalVoiceAgent orchestrator
   ├─ conversation memory
   ├─ local RAG
   ├─ permissioned tools
   ├─ barge-in / AbortSignal cancellation
   └─ independent STT / LLM / TTS scheduler lanes
   │
   ▼
LLM router
   ├─ WebLLM (Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Phi-4 Mini)
   ├─ Transformers.js text generation
   └─ Browser Prompt API
   │ streaming tokens
   ▼
SpeechChunker
   │ short phrase chunks
   ▼
TTS router
   ├─ Kokoro 82M WebGPU
   ├─ MMS-TTS
   ├─ SpeechT5
   └─ local system SpeechSynthesis
   │
   ▼
Speaker
```

## How It Works

![How It Works Diagram](media_resources/howits_works_diagram.png)

## Important latency definition

The flagship target is **1 to 2 seconds Time To First Audio (TTFA)** on warmed, certified hardware. This means the interval from a user finishing a turn until the first assistant audio begins. It is not a guarantee that an entire spoken answer completes in two seconds. Actual results depend on device, browser, model, utterance length, and GPU contention.

## Required browser VAD

The SDK uses [`@ricky0123/vad-web`](https://github.com/ricky0123/vad) as the built-in VAD implementation. The playground uses Silero VAD v5 and exposes the important tunables:

- `positiveSpeechThreshold`
- `negativeSpeechThreshold`
- `redemptionMs`
- `preSpeechPadMs`
- `minSpeechMs`
- `submitUserSpeechOnPause`
- `processorType`
- microphone constraints

`onSpeechEnd` provides the 16 kHz `Float32Array` used directly by segment STT providers.

## Quick start

Requirements:

- Node.js 22+
- Chrome or Edge recommended for WebGPU
- HTTPS in production. `localhost` is acceptable during development.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

The post-build asset step copies the VAD worklet, Silero ONNX model, and ONNX Runtime Web WASM/MJS assets into the playground so VAD does not depend on a third-party CDN at runtime.

### Production build

```bash
npm run check
npm run build
docker build -t local-voice-agent .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 local-voice-agent
```

Then open `http://localhost:8080`.

## Basic SDK usage

```ts
import { LocalVoiceAgent } from "@local-voice-agent/sdk";

const agent = await LocalVoiceAgent.create({
  mode: "ultra-fast",
  bargeIn: true,
  vad: {
    model: "v5",
    baseAssetPath: "/vad/",
    onnxWASMBasePath: "/ort/",
    positiveSpeechThreshold: 0.5,
    negativeSpeechThreshold: 0.35,
    redemptionMs: 420
  },
  stt: {
    provider: "whisper",
    model: "onnx-community/whisper-tiny.en",
    device: "wasm",
    language: "en"
  },
  llm: {
    provider: "webllm",
    model: "Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC",
    worker: true,
    cacheBackend: "cache"
  },
  tts: {
    provider: "kokoro",
    model: "onnx-community/Kokoro-82M-v1.0-ONNX",
    device: "webgpu",
    dtype: "fp32",
    voice: "af_heart"
  }
});

agent.on("metrics", console.log);
agent.on("transcript:final", console.log);
agent.on("assistant:chunk", console.log);

await agent.prepare();
await agent.start();
```

## Auto mode

```ts
const agent = await LocalVoiceAgent.create({ mode: "auto" });
```

Auto mode checks browser capabilities. It can prefer browser on-device STT when the language pack is explicitly available, otherwise it falls back to a local Transformers.js STT. LLM and TTS selection consider WebGPU and local voice support.

The SDK intentionally does **not** assume generic `SpeechRecognition` is local. The

name: alitalari/webrtc-ai-voice-agent
readmeExcerpt:
# AI Voice SDK

A from-scratch, **real-time AI voice agent** over WebRTC — talk to it, it talks back, interrupt it mid-sentence and it stops. Vendor-neutral: ASR, LLM, and TTS are pluggable adapters (defaults: **Deepgram · Claude · Cartesia**). The interesting part isn't the providers — it's the **session layer** that sits between them: server-side voice-activity detection, turn-taking, barge-in cancellation, and per-turn latency instrumentation.

**TypeScript · WebRTC (werift) · 70 passing tests · Apache-2.0 · live demo deployed**

---

## TL;DR

> The short version — read this, skim the diagram, and you've got it.

- **What it is.** A reference backend + browser client that run a full voice loop: your mic → WebRTC → server-side turn detection → ASR → LLM → TTS → the agent's voice streamed back, all in ~1–1.4 s end-to-end.
- **What's actually hard here** (and built from scratch, not bought): **endpointing** (knowing when *you* stopped talking), **turn-taking** as an explicit state machine, and **barge-in** — interrupt the agent and it cancels the in-flight LLM + TTS instantly.
- **Vendor-neutral by design.** Each provider hides behind a small adapter interface. No API key for a stage? It transparently falls back to a fake, so the whole thing runs offline with zero credentials.
- **Latency is a feature.** Every turn emits a breakdown (LLM first-token / generate / TTS) that the demo plots live, so the cost of each stage is visible instead of guessed at.
- **Real WebRTC, server-side.** ICE / DTLS / SRTP / SCTP data channel via [`werift`](https://github.com/shinyoshiaki/werift-webrtc) — not a websocket pretending to be a call.
- **Tested and deployed.** 70 unit/integration tests; running live behind TLS on a single small VPS.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alitalari/webrtc-ai-voice-agent.git && cd webrtc-ai-voice-agent
npm install && npm run build
npm start -w @voice/server          # → open http://localhost:8080 and talk
```
No API keys required for that — it boots on fake providers (a tone + canned transcript) so you can see the whole pipeline work before wiring real ones.

![End-to-end architecture and a single turn](docs/architecture-flow.png)

---

## Quickstart — clone & run

**Prerequisites:** Node ≥ 20 and a Chromium/Firefox browser (microphone access needs a secure context — `localhost` counts).

```bash
# 1. Clone
git clone https://github.com/alitalari/webrtc-ai-voice-agent.git
cd webrtc-ai-voice-agent

# 2. Install (npm workspaces) and build (tsc -b across all packages)
npm install
npm run build

# 3. Run the reference server + demo page
npm start -w @voice/server
#    → "@voice/server dev server on http://localhost:8080"

# 4. Open http://localhost:8080, click Connect, allow the mic, and talk.
```

Out of the box every stage uses a **fake provider** (the LLM returns a canned line, the TTS plays a tone), so the full WebRTC + turn-taking + barge-in loop works with **no credentials and no network**.

### Run it for real

Drop your keys into a gitignored env file and the matching stages swap from fake → real automatically:

```bash
cp apps/server/.env.example apps/server/.env
# edit apps/server/.env:
#   DEEPGRAM_API_KEY=...     (console.deepgram.com)   → real ASR
#   ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...    (console.anthropic.com)  → real LLM (Claude)
#   CARTESIA_API_KEY=...     (play.cartesia.ai)       → real TTS
npm run build && npm start -w @voice/server
```

Each key is independent — set one, two, or all three; unset stages stay on the fake. Keys are read **server-side only** and never reach the browser.

### Develop

```bash
npm run build          # tsc -b — also the typecheck
npm test               # vitest — 70 tests across 9 files
npm run test:coverage
npm run lint           # eslint (flat config)
npm run format         # prettier --check
```

A hosted instance runs behind TLS + a password gate: **https://voice.alitalari.com** (access on request). The ungated health endpoint — `…/status` — returns which pr

name: enricollen/fastRTC-voice-agent
readmeExcerpt:
# 🎙️ FastRTC Voice Agent

A model-agnostic voice-enabled AI assistant that can engage in natural conversations. The project combines FastRTC for real-time communication, multiple speech services, and LiteLLM for flexible model support.

Demo:

[![Video Title](https://img.youtube.com/vi/fjYv0PuJT7k/0.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fjYv0PuJT7k)

## ⚙️ How it Works

1. The system captures your voice input
2. Converts speech to text using your configured STT provider
3. Sends the text to your configured LLM via LiteLLM
4. Converts the response to speech using your configured TTS provider
5. Plays back the audio response

## ✨ Features

- Real-time voice conversations in multiple languages
- **Model-agnostic architecture**: Mix and match different providers for each component
- **Intelligent Agent**: LlamaIndex-powered agent with tool usage capabilities
- **Memory Management**: Token-aware conversation history with configurable limits
- Speech-to-Text: ElevenLabs, Groq, OpenAI, Whisper (local)
- Text-to-Speech: ElevenLabs, Kokoro (local)
- Web interface with custom UI or Gradio standard UI
- Fully customizable assistant persona via YAML configuration
- LLM-agnostic: easily switch between OpenAI, Gemini, Groq, Ollama, and OpenRouter
- Automatic fallback to alternative models if primary model fails
- Session-based chat history for context-aware conversations
- Clean, modular class-based architecture
- Environment variables and command-line arguments for flexible configuration

## 🏗️ Architecture

![FastRTC Architecture](docs/images/architecture.png)

The project follows a modular class-based design with multiple components working together to provide a seamless voice interaction experience:

1. **FastRTC**: Handles real-time voice communication
2. **Speech Services**:
   - **STT (Speech-to-Text)**: Supports ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Groq, and local Whisper
   - **TTS (Text-to-Speech)**: Supports ElevenLabs and local Kokoro TTS
3. **LiteLLM**: Provides unified access to multiple LLM providers:
   - OpenRouter
   - Google Gemini
   - OpenAI
   - Groq
   - Local Ollama
4. **Agent Framework**: A Llamaindex ReAct agent orchestrates the conversation flow with:
   - Weather Tool integration (example)
   - Memory management

## 🎯 Recommended Configuration

After extensive testing, the following configuration has proven to provide the best balance of latency, accuracy, and overall user experience:

- **Speech-to-Text**: ElevenLabs or Groq (both offer excellent accuracy with low latency)
- **Text-to-Speech**: ElevenLabs (best voice quality and response time)
- **LLM Provider**: Google Gemini (specifically gemini flash (1.5 or 2.5) for fastest responses while maintaining high quality)

This setup minimizes overall latency while maintaining high accuracy in speech recognition and natural-sounding responses.

Located in `config/prompts.yaml`:

The agent supports various tools that can be enabled/disabled:
```python

]

```python

MEMORY_TOKEN_LIMIT=4000        # Total memory token limit
CHAT_HISTORY_RATIO=0.8         # Ratio for chat history (80% of total)

readmeExcerpt:
# @missionsquad/browserai

Run small open AI models **entirely in the browser** with WebGPU — no inference server — as an
embeddable, UI-free TypeScript SDK. BrowserAI packages a curated 47-model catalog, model
loading/downloading with progress, capability-slot management, three inference runtimes, streaming,
schema-constrained JSON generation, run metrics, browser-cache management, and a complete
press-to-talk voice-assistant pipeline. Drop it into any frontend site and build your own UI on top.

Three inference runtimes:

- **WebLLM (MLC)** for quantized MLC text models, with schema-constrained JSON decoding and detailed
  per-token runtime telemetry.
- **Transformers.js + ONNX/WebGPU** for browser-ready ONNX models: text LLMs, Whisper/Moonshine/
  Parakeet transcription, Supertonic speech, SmolVLM/Qwen-VL/OCR vision, Gemma 4 multimodal, and
  audio-LLM ASR (Granite Speech, Voxtral realtime).
- **kokoro-js** (loaded from its CDN bundle by default) for Kokoro 82M text-to-speech, including
  sentence-by-sentence streaming synthesis.

## Install

```bash
npm install @missionsquad/browserai
```

Requirements: a WebGPU-capable browser (lightweight speech models — Whisper/Moonshine/Parakeet
transcription and the TTS engines — can fall back to wasm; text, vision, and audio-LLM models
require WebGPU), Node.js 20+ for development. `@mlc-ai/web-llm` and `@huggingface/transformers` are regular
dependencies, dynamically imported only when a model that needs them loads — your initial bundle
stays small.

## Quickstart

```ts
import { BrowserAI } from "@missionsquad/browserai";

const ai = new BrowserAI();
ai.on("loadprogress", ({ progress, status }) => console.log(progress, status));

await ai.load("Qwen3.5-0.8B-q4f16_1-MLC"); // downloads once, then serves from browser cache

const { text, stats } = await ai.generateText(
  [
    { role: "system", content: "You are terse." },
    { role: "user", content: "Why is the sky blue?" },
  ],
  { runtime: { jsonMode: "none" }, onDelta: (full) => render(full) },
);
console.log(text, stats.extra?.decode_tokens_per_s);
```

### Capability slots

Models load into one of four **capability slots** — `text`, `vision`, `stt` (transcription), `tts`
(speech) — with at most one model per slot, so up to four models can be resident at once. Loading a
model whose slots are occupied replaces the conflicting owner. Loads/unloads are single-flight, and
runs are serialized per loaded model, so concurrent calls queue instead of driving one engine from
two places.

```ts
await ai.load("onnx-community/whisper-base");          // stt slot
await ai.load("onnx-community/Kokoro-82M-v1.0-ONNX");  // tts slot

const { text } = await ai.transcribe(pcm16k);           // Float32Array @ 16 kHz mono
const clip = await ai.synthesizeToClip("Hello!", { voice: "af_heart" });
ai.occupiedSlots();                                     // Set { "text", "stt", "tts" }
```

### Schema-constrained JSON

```ts
import { buildExtractionMessages, parseJsonFromModel, validateAgainstJsonSchema } from "@missionsquad/browserai";

const messages = buildExtractionMessages(inputText, mySchema);
const { text } = await ai.generateText(messages, { schema: mySchema }); // WebLLM: real constrained decoding
const parsed = parseJsonFromModel(text);
if (parsed.ok) console.log(validateAgainstJsonSchema(parsed.value, mySchema)); // [] when valid
```

WebLLM backends enforce the schema with a grammar-constrained decoder; Transformers.js backends are
prompt-guided, so validate the output either way.

### Voice pipeline (press-to-talk assistant)

`VoicePipeline` chains mic → STT → text LLM → TTS → speakers as a headless state machine with typed
events. With Kokoro in the speech slot, replies are spoken **while the text model is still
generating** (audio starts after the first sentence); other TTS models speak the finished reply as
one clip. Pressing talk during playback stops it (barge-in).

```ts
import { BrowserAI, VoicePipeline } from "@missionsquad/browserai

# Next-Generation Open-Source Virtual Assistant NOVA

**Version 1.6**

# ⚠️The project is no longer beeing maintained due to overwhelming tech-debt. You can find the successor project [here](https://github.com/00Julian00/Nova2).

## Table of Contents
- [Introduction](#introduction)
- [Requirements](#requirements)
- [Installation](#installation)
    - [Setup](#setup)
    - [Run](#run)
- [Main Menu Commands](#main-menu-commands)
- [Settings](#settings)
- [Version History](#version-history)

## Introduction
The Next-Generation Open-Source Virtual Assistant (or NOVA) is an easily expandable and modifyable virtual assistant. It uses the [Groq API](https://groq.com) for the text transcription, as well as the processing of the query, making it fast and responsive. NOVA uses the [Elevenlabs API](https://elevenlabs.io) for rich and natural speech. NOVA can be easily expanded, using Modules. Modules can add extra functionality to the system, are modular and can be easily developed. See [here](https://github.com/00Julian00/Nova-Devtools.git) for further resources on Module development. NOVA is still under development.

## Requirements

- [Groq API key](https://groq.com)
- [Elevenlabs API key](https://elevenlabs.io)
- [Python 3.11.x with PIP](https://www.python.org)
- [mpv](https://mpv.io)
- [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html)
- [Microsoft C++ Build Tools](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/de/visual-cpp-build-tools/)
- [Cuda 12.1](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-12-1-0-download-archive)

## Installation

```bash
git clone https://github.com/00Julian00/Nova.git
cd Nova
pip3 install torch torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Setup

1. Run `Start interface.bat`.
2. Type `keys`.
3. Enter your Groq and Elevenlabs API keys.
4. Go back to the main menu.
5. Enter `micID`.
6. Find the correct microphone and remember its ID.
7. Enter `settings`.
8. Change the microphone ID to the correct ID.
9. Change other settings if necessary.

## Run

1. In the main menu, type `boot`.
2. A separate terminal will open. Wait until the boot process is complete and the Hotword detection starts.
3. You can now speak to the assistant.
4. Make sure to say the specified hotword (default is "Nova") at some point during your prompt, or it will be ignored.

## Main Menu Commands

- `help`: Show a list of all available commands
- `boot`: Start Nova
- `keys`: Edit your API keys. **Warning:** Will expose your API keys
- `settings`: Edit your settings
- `exit`: Exit the interface. Does not close any instances of Nova running
- `micID`: Lists all your microphones and their IDs. You can then set the correct ID in `settings`
- `clear`: Clear the console

## Settings

- **Language**: The language 'Nova' should use. Must be a valid language code (e.g., en, es, fr, de, etc.).
- **Hotword**: Your input will only be processed if it includes this word.
- **LanguageModel**: The LLM that should be used. Note that it is not possible to check whether your chosen model is valid, so choose a valid model. [Groq Models](https://console.groq.com/docs/models)
- **ElevenlabsModel**: The voice model that should be used for the Text-To-Speech. Note that it is not possible to check whether your chosen model is valid, so choose a valid model. [Elevenlabs Models](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/speech-synthesis/models)
- **ElevenlabsVoiceID**: The ID of the voice you want to use. You can find the IDs of the premade voices and your own voices on [Elevenlabs](https://elevenlabs.io).
- **OfflineMode (True/False)**: Run all required AI models on local hardware. No internet connection is needed, apart from first downloading the models. Switch off Offline Mode for better response times and higher quality.
- **StreamVoice (True/False)**: Do you want to stream the voice? Streaming is generally a lot faster but can lead to buffering, especially if you are not using a turbo model.
